name: DHT / Androgel for facial structure

lead: Some looksmaxxing posters promote topical DHT (dihydrotestosterone) gel to enhance brow ridge, jaw and cheek development and beard growth, especially during puberty. AndroGel is a testosterone gel approved for male hypogonadism, and discussion sometimes uses it alongside or instead of DHT gel.

The chain is local androgen action: DHT is made from testosterone by 5-alpha-reductase and acts locally in tissues, where it is linked to facial and body hair, prostate growth and male genital development. Forum proponents argue it drives facial masculinity. Human trials of gels were in older men with low testosterone, looking at well-being, sexual function, cognition and the prostate, not facial bone or adolescents.

paras: Users describe applying gel to the skin on a routine and pairing it with other facial-development ideas. Pharmaceutical DHT gel is sold in some European countries, and forum use often involves other sources.

Testosterone gels can transfer to others by contact and are reported to raise prostate-specific antigen modestly. A trial in healthy men found DHT administration did not raise intraprostatic androgen concentrations. Pharmaceutical DHT is unavailable in the US and Canada.

angle.text: Forum users apply DHT or testosterone gel during puberty hoping for a more masculine facial structure and a fuller beard. Gels have been studied for low testosterone in older men; their effect on facial bone development has not been tested.

lead: DHT gel and AndroGel for facial structure is a hormonal idea discussed on looksmaxxing forums: that applying a topical androgen, usually dihydrotestosterone (DHT) gel and sometimes testosterone gel, during or after puberty could strengthen masculine features such as the brow ridge, jaw and cheekbones, giving a more angular, dimorphic face. Proponents describe DHT as the most androgenic hormone and argue that more androgen signalling in facial tissue means more pronounced masculine structure [1][2].

DHT is an androgen made from testosterone by the enzyme 5-alpha-reductase and acts mainly inside the tissues that make it. It is linked to facial and body hair, prostate and genital development [3]. As a medication it is called androstanolone and is sold as gels, tablets and injectable esters in some European countries, but not in the US or Canada [3]. AndroGel is a brand of testosterone gel approved for male hypogonadism.

Published trials of DHT gel and testosterone gel were carried out in older men with low testosterone and looked at well-being, sexual function, mood, cognition, body composition, bone density and the prostate [4][5][6][7][8]. No published study has tested either gel for facial bone development, or in adolescents for appearance.

paras: The idea rests on DHT's role as the potent androgen of puberty. Users who discuss it online typically target adolescents or young adults whose growth is not complete, a group they call 'youngcels', and describe gel application to the skin as a route to raise androgen exposure locally [2][1].

Transdermal testosterone gels were introduced in the US in 2000 and reach steady-state testosterone levels within about 24 hours of application, without the peaks and troughs of injectable esters. Pharmaceutical DHT, sold as androstanolone and under the brand Andractim, comes as tablets, gels and injectable esters in some European countries [3].

subs.h: How DHT is made and what it does
paras: About 5 to 7 percent of testosterone is converted to DHT by 5-alpha-reductase, and two main forms of the enzyme exist, with type 2 considered the more biologically important [3]. DHT binds the androgen receptor about two to three times more tightly than testosterone, dissociates from it more slowly, and cannot be converted to oestradiol by aromatase [3]. It circulates at about one-tenth the level of testosterone and acts largely in the tissues where it is formed [3]. An alternative 'backdoor' route to DHT that bypasses testosterone was named by Richard Auchus in 2004 [3][9].

DHT is linked to genital differentiation, facial and body hair growth, prostate enlargement and scalp hair recession, whereas testosterone is linked to spermatogenesis, voice deepening, musculoskeletal development and libido [3].

People with 5-alpha-reductase type 2 deficiency have low DHT. The condition was confirmed as a human cause in 1974, from cases in the Dominican Republic and the US. At puberty affected people typically deepen their voice, gain muscle mass and have a growth spurt; bone density is normal, while facial and body hair is reduced and male-pattern baldness does not occur [10][3]. Proponents of DHT gel point to DHT's role in virilisation, and researchers describing this condition report that musculoskeletal changes of puberty proceed with low DHT [10][3].

Reviews of testosterone gel report that application-site reactions are less frequent than with patches and polycythaemia risk is lower than with injections. Secondary exposure through skin contact is a recognised challenge of gels. Wikipedia notes that women and children exposed to testosterone may develop masculinisation [11].
No studies found on topical DHT or testosterone gel for facial structure or for appearance in adolescents. Related studies concern other populations.

A randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial in 120 men aged 50 to 70 examined DHT gel for general well-being, sexual function and the prostate [4]. A registered phase 2 study tested DHT gel for symptoms of low testosterone in men aged 55 to 80, enrolling 128 participants [5]. A preliminary report examined cognitive changes with testosterone or DHT supplementation in mildly hypogonadal men [8].

A randomised trial in healthy men found that DHT administration did not increase intraprostatic androgen concentrations or alter prostate androgen action [6], and a registered phase 1/2 study of DHT's effect on prostate tissue in 31 healthy men was completed [12]. A long-term study of AndroGel in hypogonadal men for up to 42 months reported sustained effects on sexual function, mood, lean and fat mass and bone mineral density [7].

For testosterone, common adverse effects listed include acne, swelling and breast enlargement in men, and serious ones include liver toxicity, heart disease and behavioural change; testosterone can harm a baby during pregnancy or breastfeeding and is not for people with prostate cancer [11]. In February 2025 the FDA removed language about adverse cardiovascular outcomes from the testosterone boxed warning and added a warning about increased blood pressure [11].

Because DHT is linked to scalp hair recession [3], hair-related effects are a recurring topic: 5-alpha-reductase inhibitors that lower DHT are used for male pattern hair loss, and finasteride trials report hair benefits in men with androgenetic alopecia [13][3]. Those inhibitors have their own reported effects, including sexual dysfunction in about 3 to 16 percent of men and, in some reports, mood symptoms [3]. A looksmax.org member asks on a thread titled 'DHT itch' whether scalp itching after a break from finasteride is a real phenomenon [14].

A long looksmax.org post titled as an 'ultimate pubertymaxing tool' argues that topical DHT applied during puberty could enhance the development of the brow ridge, jawline and cheekbones, describing DHT as more androgenic than testosterone and non-aromatising, and saying the topic is often mocked on the forum [2]. Other threads ask about facial application and use for mandible growth [15].

Another thread, framed as an advanced guide, says DHT governs craniofacial growth, jaw definition and temporal thickening and cites mouse knockout studies and periosteal androgen-receptor signalling as mechanisms; replies in the thread include both sarcasm and disagreement, with some members arguing DHT affects mainly hair, skin and genital growth [1]. A looksmax.org thread on DHT and hair loss states that DHT is the main reason hair falls out [16].
Members of the guide thread disagree over whether DHT matters beyond hair, skin and genital growth, and the hair-loss thread treats DHT mainly as something to lower [1][16].

DHT as a drug is not available in the US or Canada but is available in some European countries [3]. Testosterone is a controlled substance in many jurisdictions: Schedule III in the US, Schedule IV in Canada, Class C in the UK, and prescription-only in the EU [11].

Looksmaxxing communities discuss DHT gel alongside testosterone replacement, finasteride and dutasteride for hair, and other puberty-timing topics. Testosterone gel for delayed puberty in boys is a medical use under specialist care [11].

lore.intro: On looksmax.org, DHT gel threads propose it as a puberty-stage tool for facial masculinisation, while other members dispute it, joke about it or focus on DHT's effect on hair [2][1][16].

claims.claim: Topical DHT during puberty enhances masculine facial bone development.
DHT is the more potent, non-aromatising option compared with testosterone.
DHT acts on facial bones through periosteal androgen receptors.
DHT gel is among the safest looksmaxxing tools.

timeline.event: Adolf Butenandt and colleagues first synthesise DHT by hydrogenating testosterone [3].
DHT is introduced medically as an anabolic-androgenic steroid [3].
DHT is identified as an endogenous substance formed from testosterone [3].
5-alpha-reductase type 2 deficiency is confirmed as a human cause of undervirilisation, clarifying DHT's functions [10][3].
Transdermal testosterone gels are introduced in the US.
A randomised placebo-controlled trial of transdermal DHT in aging men is published [4].
Richard Auchus names the backdoor pathway to DHT [3][9]; a long-term AndroGel study in hypogonadal men is published [7].
A randomised trial reports that DHT did not raise intraprostatic androgen concentrations in healthy men [6].
The FDA revises the testosterone boxed warning, removing cardiovascular outcomes language and adding a blood-pressure warning [11].
